title: Silent female representation and tech entrepreneurial project evaluation: The role of evaluators' genders
authors: Yan “Anthea” Zhang; Lun Li; Jizhen Li; Xiwei Yi
affiliations: School of Business Rice University Houston Texas USA; Business School Beijing Normal University Beijing China; School of Economics and Management Tsinghua University Beijing China; Guanghua School of Management Peking University Beijing China
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We examine how the nature of female representation in tech entrepreneurial projects may be related to the evaluations of the projects. We argue that silent female representation —i.e., women are present but do not speak in representing projects—may reinforce the stereotyped view of women, resulting in lower project evaluations relative to male‐only projects, whereas active female representation may not lead to evaluation penalty. We further predict that the negative association between silent female representation and project evaluation is stronger when the evaluators are women than when they are men. Conducted in a unique setting wherein female and male evaluators on panels, independently and confidentially, rated funding applications represented by various mixes of male and female entrepreneurs, our study provides evidence that is consistent with these predictions. Managerial Summary It is widely recognized that female entrepreneurs face greater challenges than their male counterparts when seeking external financial resources in the tech sector. This funding disparity may start from evaluation disparity. We find that projects with silent female representation—i.e., women are present but do not speak—receive lower evaluations than male‐only projects, whereas projects with active female representation receive evaluations comparable to male‐only projects. We also find that female evaluators are more likely than male evaluators to penalize projects with silent female representation. Our research offers valuable insights into strategies for fostering gender equality in traditionally male‐dominated fields.

title: Should birds of a feather flock together: How public criticism shapes pressures for sustainability conformity and differentiation
authors: Nareuporn (Bell) Piyasinchai; Matthew Grimes
affiliations: Department of Organization Studies Tilburg University Tilburg the Netherlands; Cambridge Judge Business School University of Cambridge Cambridge UK
abstract: Abstract Research Summary While firms face pressure to engage in Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) practices, it is unclear how they should specifically engage given the breadth of sustainability‐related concerns. Drawing on optimal distinctiveness and social evaluations research, we argue that public criticism directed toward an industry creates oscillating pressures for firms to conform with or deviate from industry ESG norms. Using data on 8176 global companies from 2013 to 2022, we find that although ESG conformity benefits investor evaluations, once industry peers' public criticism accumulates beyond a threshold, ESG differentiation is rewarded, particularly when firms increase material ESG practices and reduce immaterial ones. Our study reveals how public criticism dynamically reshapes the evaluative processes by which investors determine firm legitimacy, bridging optimal distinctiveness and social evaluations literatures. Managerial Summary Our research indicates that firms often adopt similar ESG practices as their industry peers, which usually enhances investor evaluations. However, this conformity can backfire and become a liability when industry peers face significant criticism. In such scenarios, firms that adopt distinctive ESG practices compared to the industry tend to receive greater rewards, especially when differentiation involves increasing material ESG practices and reducing immaterial ones. Therefore, while adopting ESG norms can be beneficial, managers should be vigilant of public opinion and ready to deviate from those norms when necessary.

title: Temporal tradeoffs and contracting dynamics in buyer–supplier agreements
authors: Jeffrey J. Reuer; Toby X. Li
affiliations: Mitch Daniels School of Business Purdue University West Lafayette Indiana USA; Mays Business School Texas A&M University College Station Texas USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We examine temporal tradeoffs and contracting dynamics in buyer–supplier agreements by investigating how suppliers' contractual terms change when contracting with initial clients versus new clients in the future. We use information economics and research on certifications in interorganizational relationships to delve into the mechanisms leading to potential improvements in suppliers' contractual terms. We situate the empirical analysis in the context of onshore oil and gas drilling projects to examine the liabilities for project‐related risks that startup drillers assume when contracting with client producers. Evidence indicates that when drillers initially work for prominent client producers, the drillers assume more risks in these first contracts, but fewer risks in subsequent agreements with other client producers. We argue and show that the degree to which a specific driller obtains better terms in future deals owing to its initial client's prominence will be attenuated when subsequent clients have more information on the value of the driller's resources and capabilities. Specifically, the resulting reduction in risks borne by the driller will be smaller when the driller was founded by a serial entrepreneur and when the subsequent client is vertically integrated into drilling operations. Managerial Summary This study examines the contracting dynamics that startups experience as suppliers in buyer–supplier agreements. Startups often bear more risk in initial deals to build credibility, especially when contracting with prominent clients, and such affiliations can then lead to improved terms for startups in subsequent contracts with other clients. However, this follow‐on benefit of working with a prominent client depends upon whether subsequent clients have more information on the startup's resources and capabilities. In particular, the risk‐reduction effect of working with an initial client that is prominent will be smaller for those startups founded by serial entrepreneurs. It will also be smaller when the subsequent client is vertically integrated into the value chain activities carried out by the startup. Using data from startups in the oil and gas drilling industry, we illustrate the dynamics and tradeoffs that startup drillers encounter when contracting with established client producers.

title: Rising Wages and the Decline of Low-Wage Work
authors: Clem Aeppli; Soohyun Roh; Nathan Wilmers
affiliations: MIT
abstract: From 2014 to 2024, the share of U.S. hourly workers paid below $15 in real terms fell by two-thirds, from 38 percent to 13 percent. Why? We first distinguish the entry and exit of employers—wherein high-paying employers have supplanted low-paying ones—from organizational changes among incumbent employers. Organizational changes can be imposed on employers by external constraints, like labor market tightness, or emerge from the pursuit of new opportunities. Using panel data drawn from administrative records and job reviews, we bring this framework to bear on the recent wage gains at the bottom of the labor market. Contrary to predictions of creative destruction, we can trace only a small amount of these wage gains to the disappearance of low-wage organizations. Instead, the main driver of rising pay was low- and middle-paying incumbent employers of low-wage occupations increasing pay. These gains in low-wage occupations were associated with tightening labor markets and increased minimum wages. But over and above these external constraints, employers also pursued new opportunities for reorganizing work in low-skill jobs. Notwithstanding organizational inertia, major gains for workers’ pay can come from changes in existing workplaces.

Influence Without Authority: Bottom-Up Normalization of Organizational Corruption
authors: Patricia Helena Hein; Shahzad (Shaz) Ansari
affiliations: Western University, Ivey Business School, London, Canada; University of Cambridge, Judge Business School, Cambridge, Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
abstract: Research on organizational corruption has largely portrayed normalization as a top-down, management-driven process. We know less about how employees with limited formal authority can escalate wrongdoing beyond isolated acts and drive its normalization. Drawing on a qualitative study of a German recruitment firm’s practices during the COVID-19 pandemic, we develop a three-phase model of bottom-up normalization of organizational wrongdoing. Less powerful actors first engage in tolerated rule-bending to demonstrate competence and indispensability and build influence through informal networks. When disruption threatens this influence and legitimate alternatives are unavailable, they may escalate to more serious wrongdoing to safeguard their standing by framing new opportunities as extensions of familiar rule-bending. Normalization then depends on their ability to sustain a cohesive coalition, secure support from actors with formal authority, and contain resistance. We make three contributions. First, we advance a relational view of corruption by showing how central positions in informal networks enable actors lacking formal authority to mobilize support across hierarchical levels and normalize wrongdoing. Second, we show how organizational corruption can become a means of building and preserving social influence, fostering a sense of accomplishment rather than guilt or shame. Third, we identify a disruption-driven pathway to normalization in which threats to less powerful actors’ social influence precipitate abrupt escalation from tolerated rule-bending to more serious wrongdoing.

title: Decision Considerations Influencing Information Systems Modularity: A Multimethod Study of LEGO
authors: Stefan Henningsson; Ben Eaton; Lorenz Törmer; Suprateek Sarker
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School, Digitalization, Frederiksberg, Capital Region, Denmark; Copenhagen Business School, Department of Digitalization, Frederiksberg, 2000, Denmark; University of Virginia McIntire School of Commerce, Information Technology, Charlottesville, Virginia, United States
abstract: Abstract. The maturing of concepts such as microservices and open application programming interfaces (APIs) has radically increased the practicality of fine-grained modularization in Information Systems (IS) architecture. These are critical technical advancements, given the central role of modularity in the ability of IS to transform and meet future organizational needs efficiently. Nevertheless, reports from practice suggest that, when presented with new opportunities for modularization, organizations face multifaceted decision criteria and do not necessarily embrace new approaches as may be expected. While emergent IS literature observes that organizations’ decisions on modularity in IS may involve competing concerns, understanding of the considerations involved and how they influence such decisions remains limited. To examine these considerations, we intensively study the experience of LEGO, a global toy company. Specifically, we sequentially apply multiple methods consisting of an exploratory inductive analysis of LEGO’s approach to IS modularity decisions over 36 months, which then informs a crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) of 31 episodes of LEGO’s situated decision-making on IS modularity. Through the analysis, we find the rationale for a purposeful choice between two forms of modularity that differ in granularity of decomposition, rather than a linear pursuit of maximizing decomposability in IS architecture. We bring to the fore a perspective of IS modularity as situated decisions reconciling competing demands in pursuit of the right type of modularity, in the right place to achieve the right effect. Our findings add nuance to modularity in the context of IS architecture and explain the complex causality of IS modularity decisions.

title: Online Review Generation in the Digital Age: A Meta-Analytic Study of Online Review Behavior
authors: Hong Hong; DaPeng Xu; Xiaoquan (Michael) Zhang
affiliations: Harbin Institute of Technology, School of Management, Harbin, China; Tsinghua University, Shenzhen International Graduate School, Shenzhen, China; Chinese University of Hong Kong, Decision Sciences and Managerial Economics, Shatin, N.T., CUHK Business School, Hong Kong
abstract: A large body of literature on online review generation has investigated various antecedents to online review characteristics. However, the mixed and even contradictory findings in this domain have hampered a clear understanding of consumers’ online review behavior for both researchers and practitioners, thereby complicating actionable strategies. To address this issue, we conduct a comprehensive meta-analysis of 154 independent samples from 152 empirical papers, synthesizing the relationships between 28 antecedent factors and 12 review features, which we categorize into rating-based (evaluative) and non-rating (expressive) dimensions. Our results indicate that rating attributes are dominantly driven by stable reviewer tendencies and market-level reputation cues, whereas non-rating features—such as text length and image inclusion—are primarily influenced by reviewer social embeddedness and platform engagement. Crucially, we identify that inconsistencies in prior literature can be explained by critical boundary conditions, including platform type (business-hosted vs. third-party), goods type (service vs. tangible), and cultural background (Asia vs. North America). By distinguishing between evaluative and expressive review components, our study reconciles mixed findings and uncovers underlying mechanisms such as expectation-based evaluation and self-presentation. The findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for empirical model specification and offer actionable insights for retailers and platforms to optimize reputation management and system design. Ultimately, our work offers a holistic framework for understanding online review behavior and proposes a rich agenda for future research in the digital marketplace.

title: Examining Negative Asymmetry in Employee Social Networks: A Meta-Analysis
authors: Kameron M. Carter; Hamed Ghahremani; Eean R. Crawford; Prasad Balkundi; Robert J. Barrett
affiliations: Old Dominion University; Louisiana State University New Orleans; University of Iowa; University at Buffalo (SUNY); Midway University
abstract: Two decades have passed since Labianca and Brass introduced social ledger theory with its focal assumption of negative asymmetry—that the social liabilities created by negative workplace ties are more strongly related to employee outcomes than the social assets created by positive workplace ties. Yet widespread conclusions that negative workplace ties are more consequential have exceeded a surprisingly limited base of empirical tests. This article uses meta-analysis to examine this largely untested assumption by offering 22 original meta-analytic estimates drawn from 248 effect sizes across 71 samples representing 13,369 employees. At the bivariate level, both positive and negative ties have significant relationships with employee outcomes. However, evidence consistent with negative asymmetry emerged only for out-degree ties predicting task performance. In contrast, evidence more consistent with positive asymmetry emerged for in-degree ties predicting task performance and for both in-degree and out-degree ties predicting organizational attachment, although the relationships between in-degree ties and attachment are relatively small. Considerable variation exists around the effect sizes constituting these patterns, suggesting that future research is needed to consider moderating factors that may shift the relative importance of negative versus positive ties. We discuss the implications for refining social ledger theory and for helping practitioners managing social assets and liabilities in organizations.

title: Production Function Estimation With Factor‐Augmenting Technology: An Application to Markups
authors: Mert Demirer
affiliations: Sloan School of Management, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
abstract: I develop a new method for estimating production functions with labor‐augmenting technology and apply it to markup estimation. The method imposes limited parametric restrictions and generalizes prior approaches that rely on the CES production function. I first extend the canonical Olley–Pakes framework assumptions to multidimensional productivity and then develop an identification strategy based on a control variable approach and first‐order conditions. I use this method to estimate output elasticities and markups in manufacturing industries in the US and four developing countries. I find that neglecting labor‐augmenting productivity underestimates capital elasticity, overestimates variable input elasticity, and overestimates markups in all countries.

title: Intermediate Input Substitutability
authors: Alessandra Peter; Cian Ruane
affiliations: Department of Economics, New York University; Irish Economic Analysis Division, Economics and Statistics Department, Central Bank of Ireland
abstract: We estimate long‐run elasticities of substitution between intermediate inputs for Indian manufacturing plants. India's trade liberalization in the early 1990s provides an ideal natural policy experiment, with permanent and heterogeneous tariff reductions inducing changes in relative prices which we use for identification. We find a high degree of substitutability at the plant‐level between 8 broad categories of material inputs, significantly above the Cobb–Douglas benchmark of 1. In contrast, when considering shorter time horizons or more transitory shocks to relative prices, we find evidence of much lower elasticities. Using our long‐run elasticities in a quantitative model, we find that misallocation of intermediate inputs causes a reduction in aggregate output of 29%–3.5 times larger relative to a standard calibration with complementary inputs.

title: Comment on ‘Selection and Comparative Advantage in Technology Adoption’ by Tavneet Suri
authors: Emilia Tjernström; Dalia Ghanem; Aleksandr Michuda; Oscar Barriga-Cabanillas; Travis J. Lybbert; Jeffrey D. Michler
affiliations: Department of Economics, Macquarie University; Monash Business School; Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics, University of California, Davis; Department of Economics, Swarthmore College; Poverty and Equity Global Practice, The World Bank; Department of Agricultural and Applied Economics, University of Arizona
abstract: This paper illustrates and addresses weak identification in the correlated random coefficient (CRC) model that Suri (2011) uses to study agricultural technology adoption. Using the publicly available data set, which differs slightly from the version used in Suri (2011), we obtain different point estimates for the paper's main CRC model. To understand why these differences are as large as they are, we recast the CRC model as a more general random coefficient model in which the returns to hybrid adoption are restricted to be linear in comparative advantage. This reveals that the key structural parameter in the CRC model ( ϕ ), which governs the relationship between baseline productivity and the returns to adoption, is prone to a weak‐identification problem. We then propose a procedure to conduct weak‐identification robust inference on ϕ using test inversion. Our weak‐identification robust confidence intervals contain the original Suri (2011) point estimates, which suggests that the difference in results may be attributable to a combination of minor data differences and weak identification.

title: Informal Redistribution Through Work
authors: Elisa Macchi; Jeremia Stalder
affiliations: Department of Economics, Brown University; Department of Economics, University of St. Gallen
abstract: We investigate work as informal redistribution, leveraging field experiments and firm‐level survey data from Kampala, Uganda. Employers and workers consistently choose redistribution through work over cash transfers, revealing a willingness to pay for work. By randomizing work tasks—some designed to have zero marginal product—we find that production value does not explain these choices: employers pay for zero‐value work. These patterns are also inconsistent with other relational benefits, such as social image concerns or networking. Instead, motivations are normative. Experimental evidence reveals an internalized norm for redistribution through work rooted in incentive arguments on the demand side—as employers stop requiring work only when workers have verifiable emergencies—and in reciprocity and dignity from earning on the supply side. The norm shapes both the organization and measurement of production: failing to account for redistribution through work makes firms appear significantly larger and less productive than they are.

title: Extreme Value Theory With Heterogeneous Agents
authors: Sephorah Mangin
affiliations: Research School of Economics, Australian National University
abstract: Extreme value processes feature in any economic model in which agents receive a number of draws from some distribution of values and we examine the behavior of the maximum value in the limit as the number of draws becomes large. This paper asks: Do the average outcomes of such processes change when different agents receive a different number of draws? To answer this, we allow the number of draws an agent receives from the underlying distribution of values (e.g., productivities, ideas, or utility shocks) to be given by a search technology , which reflects heterogeneity in the expected number of draws across different types of agents. We derive a new class of extreme value distributions that generalizes the three standard distributions (Fréchet, Gumbel, Weibull) by incorporating heterogeneity across agents. We generalize a result from Gabaix, Laibson, Li, Li, Resnick, and de Vries (2016) regarding extreme value outcomes and consider applications to aggregate productivity, markups, and social networks.

title: Two‐Sided Markets Shaped by Platform‐Guided Search
authors: Kwok Hao Lee; Leon Musolff
affiliations: Department of Strategy and Policy, National University of Singapore (NUS) Business School; Business Economics and Public Policy Department, The Wharton School, The University of Pennsylvania
abstract: This paper investigates concerns that vertically integrated platforms like Amazon steer demand toward their own offers via algorithmic prominence, potentially harming consumers. On Amazon, for each product, the Buybox prominence algorithm selects one seller to feature, influencing which offers consumers consider. Using novel Amazon sales and Buybox (prominence) data, we estimate a structural model capturing the effects of such algorithmic prominence on consumer choices, seller pricing, and entry. We find that the platform can indeed steer demand as 95% of consumers consider only the Buybox offer. The Buybox is highly price‐elastic (−21), but skews toward Amazon's own offers, which are featured as frequently as observably similar offers priced 5% cheaper. Still, as consumers prefer these offers, this skew does not amount to self‐preferencing in the sense of harming consumers: consumer surplus is roughly maximized at the estimated Amazon Buybox advantage, which balances higher prices against showing consumers their preferred offers.

title: An Exact t ‐Test
authors: Guillaume A. Pouliot
affiliations: Department of Economics, Rice University
abstract: Multivariate linear regression and randomization‐based inference are two essential methods in statistics and econometrics. Nevertheless, the problem of producing a randomized test for the value of a single regression coefficient that is exactly valid when errors are exchangeable, and which is asymptotically valid for the best linear predictor, has remained elusive. In this paper, we produce a test that is exactly valid with exchangeable errors and which allows for general covariate designs; covariates may be continuous as well as discrete and may be correlated. The test is asymptotically valid when the errors are not exchangeable, in particular in the presence of conditional heteroskedasticity.

affiliations: Department of Economics, Oxford University; Department of Economics, Brooks School of Public Policy, Cornell University; NBER; Busara Center for Behavioral Economics; Department of Economics, University of California, Berkeley; CEGA, University of California, Berkeley; Department of Economics, University of California, San Diego

title: From Predictive Algorithms to the Automatic Generation of Anomalies
authors: Sendhil Mullainathan; Ashesh Rambachan
affiliations: Department of Economics and Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, MIT; NBER; Department of Economics, MIT
abstract: How can we extract theoretical insights from machine learning algorithms? We take a familiar lesson: researchers often turn intuition into theoretical insight by constructing “anomalies”—specific examples highlighting hypothesized flaws in a theory, such as the Allais paradox. We develop procedures that replace researchers' intuitions with predictive algorithms: given a predictive algorithm and a theory, our procedures automatically generate anomalies for that theory. We illustrate our procedures by generating anomalies for expected utility theory. Based on a neural network that accurately predicts lottery choices, we recover known anomalies for expected utility theory and discover novel ones. In incentivized experiments, subjects violate expected utility theory on these algorithmically generated anomalies at rates similar to the Allais paradox and common ratio effect.

title: Why Are the Wealthiest so Wealthy? New Longitudinal Empirical Evidence and Implications for Theories of Wealth Inequality
authors: Joachim Hubmer; Elin Halvorsen; Sergio Salgado; Serdar Ozkan
affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Pennsylvania; Research Department, Statistics Norway; The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania; Research Division, FRB of St. Louis; Department of Economics, Southern Methodist University
abstract: We study the lifecycle dynamics of wealth inequality using 1993–2019 Norwegian administrative panel data on wealth and income. Employing a novel budget‐constraint approach, we decompose the excess wealth of the top 0.1% households relative to the median between ages 45 and 64 into higher saving rates (36%), inheritances (31%), returns (28%), and labor income (5%). One‐quarter of the wealthiest—the “New Money”—start with negative wealth on average but accumulate rapidly through high labor income and exceptionally high saving rates and returns. The “Old Money” inherit substantial wealth and grow it through above‐average though more modest saving and returns. We use these dynamic facts to evaluate five standard wealth inequality models. Although these models match cross‐sectional wealth concentration, they fail to reproduce the distinct dynamics of New and Old Money. A heterogeneous entrepreneurship model with decreasing returns to scale technology and nonhomothetic preferences is consistent with the observed dynamics.

title: Coalitions in Repeated Games
authors: S. Nageeb Ali; Ce Liu
affiliations: Department of Economics, Pennsylvania State University; Department of Economics, Michigan State University
abstract: This paper proposes a framework and solution concept for repeated coalitional behavior. We model history‐dependent schemes that use continuation promises and punishments to deter coalitions from blocking. We evaluate the effectiveness of these schemes with and without transferable utility, and apply the framework to study the implications of wage transparency in labor markets.

title: Putting the ‘Finance’ Into ‘Public Finance’: A Theory of Capital Gains Taxation
authors: Mark Aguiar; Benjamin Moll; Florian Scheuer
affiliations: Department of Economics, Princeton University; Department of Economics, London School of Economics; Department of Economics, University of Zurich
abstract: Standard optimal capital tax theory abstracts from modeling asset prices, making it unsuitable for thinking about capital gains and wealth taxation. We study optimal redistributive taxation in an environment with asset‐price movements, adopting the modern finance view that asset prices fluctuate not only because of changing cash flows, but also due to other factors (“discount rates”). We show that a combination of realization‐based capital gains and cash flow taxes implements the optimal allocation regardless of the source of asset‐price fluctuations. Moreover, the capital gains tax avoids distortions in portfolio choice (the so‐called lock‐in effect) by targeting total net trades rather than gains from selling individual assets. These results stand in contrast to the classic Haig–Simons comprehensive income tax concept as well as recent proposals for wealth or accrual‐based capital gains taxes.

title: Optimal Formula Instruments
authors: Kirill Borusyak; Peter Hull
affiliations: Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics, University of California, Berkeley; Department of Economics, Brown University
abstract: When estimating the effects of treatments defined by complex formulas, researchers often use simple functions of exogenous shocks as instruments. A leading example is “simulated instruments” for public policy eligibility, which capture variation in state‐level policy generosity. We show how more powerful instruments can be constructed by incorporating heterogeneous shock exposure while using a recentering procedure to avoid bias. We characterize the asymptotically efficient instruments in this class and propose an algorithm for constructing feasible approximations to them. Compared to a simulated instrument approach, our approach yields a 44% smaller standard error on the private insurance crowd‐out effect of Medicaid enrollment from the 2014 Affordable Care Act expansions.

title: The Social Learning Barrier
authors: Florian Brandl
affiliations: Institute for Microeconomics, Department of Economics, University of Bonn
abstract: Long‐lived agents interact repeatedly in a social network. In each period, each agent observes a private signal, chooses an action, and then observes the actions of her neighbors. We show that the learning rate of the slowest‐learning agent is capped by a constant that depends only on the distribution of the most informative private signal, but not on the number of agents, the network structure, correlations between the private signals, or the agents' strategies. For equilibrium learning with rational agents, the same result bounds the learning rate of every agent in any equilibrium under a broad class of conditions. The result is driven by an information‐theoretic tradeoff between optimal action choices and information revelation.

title: Risk Assessment and Mitigation for International Multimodal Container Transport Networks Under Compound Flood and Tropical Cyclone Events
authors: Yifan Zhu; Mengqiao Xu; Ran Yan
affiliations: School of Economics and Management Dalian University of Technology Dalian Liaoning China; School of Civil and Environmental Engineering Nanyang Technological University Singapore Singapore
abstract: ABSTRACT International multimodal container transport networks (IMCTNs) play a critical role in supporting modern logistics systems and global trade, yet they are increasingly exposed to the risk of climate extremes, particularly compound flood and tropical cyclone (TC) events. The cross‐modal impact of such events and the resulting systemic risk to IMCTNs remain insufficiently understood. This study proposes a comprehensive methodological framework for assessing and mitigating risks in IMCTNs under compound flood‐TC events. By integrating multimodal transport and multisource data with climate hazard information, the framework enables probabilistic simulations of compound events ranging from frequent disturbances to rare extreme events and multi‐scale risk quantification at both the network and county levels. The framework proposes multiple component reinforcement strategies based on their criticality and disaster‐specific failure characteristics, thereby informing the design of targeted risk mitigation strategies. Applying the framework to a real‐world IMCTN in Mainland China, the results show that the relationship between network performance losses and events of different exceedance probabilities varies across probability ranges. Moreover, spatial heterogeneity is observed in that identical event probabilities lead to divergent losses across counties, which highlights the need for stratified monitoring frameworks for risk management. Finally, risk mitigation strategies accounting for both segment criticality and failure characteristics achieve superior effectiveness. The findings offer actionable guidance for risk mitigation in IMCTNs.

title: When One Case Feels Riskier Than One Hundred Cases: A New Framing Effect in Risk Communication
authors: Xin Liu; Rui Zheng
affiliations: Faculty of Psychology Shandong Normal University Jinan China; State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Science and Mental Health Institute of Psychology Chinese Academy of Sciences Beijing China; Department of Psychology University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Beijing China
abstract: ABSTRACT Time‐based rates are widely used in risk communication, yet little is known about how their framing shapes perception and behavior. This article distinguishes between two common frames of rate—the average‐time frame (e.g., “one death every 30 seconds”) and the average‐outcome frame (e.g., “two deaths every minute”). Four studies were conducted to examine the rate framing effects on perceived risk and behavioral intention. A pilot text analysis of Weibo posts showed that the average‐time frame was relatively more prevalent in COVID‐19 risk communication and generated higher user engagement. Across three studies ( N = 979), we found that the average‐time frame elicited higher perceived risk than the average‐outcome frame, and such a rate framing effect weakened as the objective risk level increased. Moreover, framing information in an average‐time format effectively promoted intentions to limit sedentary behavior. These findings identify a new framing effect in risk communication and offer practical implications for designing persuasive public health messages.

title: “Unseen and unheard”: Recognition and Its Role in Shaping Administrative Burden
authors: Noam Tarshish
affiliations: University of Haifa, Mount Carmel School of Social Work, , Haifa, 3498838,
abstract: Abstract Administrative burden scholarship has identified psychological costs alongside learning and compliance costs, yet the category remains homogeneous, grouping stigma, diminished autonomy, and stress, without a shared organizing principle. This article advances a mechanism-level account centered on recognition, drawing on a qualitative case study of claiming disability benefits in Israel, based on in-depth interviews with 33 individuals (16 young adults with diagnosed mental health conditions and 17 social and outreach workers). We argue that recognition, and its denial, are part of the mechanism through which psychological costs are produced, and that whether an encounter carries a message about a person's standing sorts the category into three analytically distinct types. Affective costs are emotional responses to procedural load and involve no recognition; primary symbolic costs are emotional responses to status positioning; and secondary symbolic costs arise when procedural load itself carries a message about standing. The latter two, in which recognition is at stake, are traced through Honneth's three spheres of rights, solidarity, and care, each producing its own configuration of costs. The types differ in their causes and remedies, with affective costs calling for efficiency reforms and symbolic costs for recognition-oriented ones. Social workers emerge as allies who counter misrecognition, and drawing on these findings we propose bureaucratic recognition, the building of voice, certainty, and validation into procedural design, as a remedy for status-related costs. Finally, misrecognition both constitutes symbolic costs and compounds others, positioning status, alongside distribution, as a critical axis of administrative burden.

title: From Dysfunction to Socially Embedded Adaptation: A Constructive Pathway for Jealousy Toward Creativity in the Workplace
authors: Zhuofan Kan; Jin Nam Choi; Sun Young Sung
affiliations: School of Business Nanjing University Nanjing China; College of Business Administration Seoul National University Seoul South Korea
abstract: ABSTRACT Building on growing interest in social emotions in the workplace, this study examines the social cognitive pathway through which workplace jealousy can contribute to employee creativity. Drawing on social functional theory of emotion, we propose that workplace jealousy increases the focal person's recognition of others' ideas, which subsequently promotes creative performance. Furthermore, we hypothesize that political skills, such as social astuteness and networking ability, strengthen the indirect effect of workplace jealousy on employee creativity via the recognition of others' ideas. To test our hypotheses, we conducted three studies (Study 1: field data from 269 employees and their supervisors; Study 2: an online study based on the critical incident technique involving 276 working adults; and Study 3: a scenario‐based online experiment with 278 participants). Across the three studies, our analysis provides consistent patterns that workplace jealousy has a significant positive indirect effect on employee creativity via the recognition of others' ideas. Our analysis also shows that political skills strengthen this indirect relationship, although the results varied across the two dimensions. These results provide valuable theoretical insights into the constructive social functions of workplace jealousy toward creative processes, particularly for employees who are politically skilled.

title: Perspectives: A Tale of Three Plots: Advancing narrative theorising in organisation and management research
authors: Nele Langebraun; Bareerah Hafeez Hafeez Hoorani; Emmanuella Plakoyiannaki; Michael Gibbert; Joep Cornelissen
affiliations: HES-SO University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland; Institute of Marketing and Corporate Communication/ Università della Svizzera italiana, Lugano
abstract: Narrative theorising (rather than theorising based on constructs and models) is much called for in qualitative research in management and organisation studies. Despite this, how to emplot, i.e. the process of configuring fragmented events into coherent and meaningful accounts with the objective of sensemaking and understanding remains underexplored. This Perspectives piece showcases recent exemplars illustrating how we can practice narrative theorising using three distinct styles: historical, metaphorical, and discursive narratives. Since narrative theorising is commonly observed in single-case studies, we begin our exploration by drawing on six such articles published in Organization Studies to demonstrate how these styles foreground the temporal evolution of phenomena, bridge between multiple divergent accounts, or highlight conflicts between competing discourses to construct theoretical accounts and understanding. We illustrate each style in terms of its distinctive form, set of paradigmatic assumptions, analytical moves, and intended aims, with the overall aim of advancing the potential of narrative theorising in organisation and management research.

title: Constituting Technological Stigma: The Oscillating Stigmatization of Internal Combustion Engine Scooters
authors: I-lun Tsai; Ru-Mei Hsieh
abstract: Technologies can themselves become objects of stigmatization, rather than merely serving as vehicles through which stigma is directed at associated individuals or organizations. As technologies evolve, shifts in their benefits and harms may alter the grounds for stigma. Yet it remains unclear how these shifts shape stigma trajectories. We examine this issue through a longitudinal qualitative study of the stigmatization of internal combustion engine (ICE) scooters in Taiwan (2009–2021), a case in which a proposal to phase them out in favor of electric scooters was later withdrawn. We show how stigmatizing and stigmatized audiences, evolving technologies, and infrastructures co-constitute evaluative conditions that shape which attributes and consequences acquire discrediting significance. Stigma first attached to legacy ICE models and then spread to all ICE scooters. Its scope later narrowed as upgraded variants regained acceptance, although legacy models remained discredited. This oscillating trajectory unfolds through three mechanisms: constituting a graded technological order, polarizing this order, and reconstituting technological normality. Our model thus extends audience-centered accounts by explaining how human and nonhuman elements jointly shape the trajectory and scope of technology stigma.

title: Temporal Intuition and Organization Studies: Surfacing Intangible Time from a Sea Kayak
authors: Tor Hernes
abstract: Scholarship on organisational temporality has yet to fully take into account intangible time, defined in this essay as the creative connecting of fragmented temporal experiences through ‘temporal intuition’. This essay argues for a stronger attention to temporal intuition to enrich current understandings of temporal forms in organization studies. Inspired by Bergson’s work on lived temporal experience, it reports from the author’s direct experience of time during a 15-day solo sea-kayaking journey from Copenhagen to Oslo in August 2025. It shows how the experience of paddling in challenging weather and sea conditions required continued reliance on intuition to connect the multiple and dispersed temporal experiences encountered during the trip. Retrospective reflection on this experience has yielded three forms of temporal experience that can inspire further temporal theorizing: immanent events, inchoate rhythm, and contemporaneous flows. The essay concludes with suggestions on how to give temporal intuition a voice in organization studies by developing empirical, methodological and analytical aspects, thereby bringing intangible time from obscurity.

title: Ethical bricolage as ethics-as-practice in criminal organizations. The case of a drug dealing gang
authors: Thomas Sorreda; Xavier Philippe; Jean-Philippe Bouilloud
abstract: In this paper, we explore how ethics emerge in contexts of criminal organizations. To do so, we carried out a non-participant observation of a suburban drug dealing gang. Resorting to Lévi-Strauss’ concept of “bricolage”, we posit that actors assemble and recombine available moral resources in practice. We found that the criminals we studied resorted to various practices of ethical bricolage, which we define as a genuine mode of social organizing resulting from individuals collectively mobilizing and recombining available moral resources to promote situated ethical practices aimed at designing and maintaining a delineated moral territory. We contribute to the ethics-as-practice literature in discussing how, in organizations lacking social acceptability, ethical bricolage constitutes a mode of organizing, structuring the boundaries of a “man-made” acceptable life.

title: Bound to grow? How firms can thrive without growth in capitalist market environments
authors: Swantje Freund; Josua Oll; Joern Hoppmann
affiliations: University of Oldenburg, Germany; ETH Zurich, Switzerland
abstract: In capitalist market environments, firms face strong growth pressures resulting from improved access to external financing, economies of scale and scope, network effects and market power as well as enhanced career opportunities for employees. However, ecological and social challenges increasingly constrain unbounded firm growth, creating a tension between economic pressure and sustainability limits to growth. Yet, to date, both the extant literature on firm growth and the literature on post-growth and degrowth provide limited insights into how firms can thrive without growth in capitalist market environments that pressure them to grow. In this paper, we therefore investigate this question by drawing on an inductive, multiple-case study of firms pursuing different business models in the German information technology industry. We show that, to thrive without growth, firms can adopt four major strategies: patient capital, service, niche and mission orientation. Importantly, our analysis also reveals four underlying mechanisms—namely strengthening firms’ financial autonomy, using labour-intensive activities, differentiating products in the market and thriving on employee self-motivation—through which these non-growth strategies help firms compensate for the benefits typically associated with growth. By developing a theoretical framework that explicates the detailed mechanisms of how firms can thrive without growth within the dominant capitalist system, we make important contributions to the literatures on post- and degrowth and alternative forms of organising, as well as to the management literature on firm growth and non-growing firms.

title: An interior-point algorithm for continuous nonlinearly constrained optimization with noisy function and derivative evaluations
authors: Frank E. Curtis; Shima Dezfulian; Andreas Waechter
abstract: Abstract An algorithm based on the interior-point methodology for solving continuous nonlinearly constrained optimization problems is proposed, analyzed, and tested. The distinguishing feature of the algorithm is that it presumes that only noisy values of the objective and constraint functions and their first-order derivatives are available. The algorithm is based on a combination of a previously proposed interior-point algorithm that allows inexact subproblem solutions and recently proposed algorithms for solving bound- and equality-constrained optimization problems with only noisy function and derivative values. It is shown that the new interior-point algorithm drives a stationarity measure below a threshold that depends on bounds on the noise in the function and derivative values. The results of numerical experiments show that the algorithm is effective across a wide range of problems.

title: CEOs’ job-hopping experience and supply chain relationships: insights from the attention-based view
authors: Fujuan Zhang; Yang Huang; Fangzhou Song; Yongjia Lin; Shuiquan Jiang
affiliations: School of Economics, Sichuan University , ,; Macau University of Science and Technology The Institute for Sustainable Development, , ,; School of Business, Macau University of Science and Technology , ,; School of Accounting, Chongqing Technology and Business University , ,
abstract: Purpose Drawing on the attention-based view, this study examines how CEOs’ job-hopping experience shapes supply chain relationships through managerial attention to supplier search and market expansion, and how CEOs’ R&D and production-line experience moderate these effects. Design/methodology/approach Using Chinese A-share listed firms from 2012 to 2024, this study hand-codes CEOs’ job-hopping experience from resumes and measures supplier and customer concentration based on disclosed top-five trading partner shares. We use fixed-effects models, mechanism and moderation tests and a series of robustness and endogeneity analyses. Findings Firms led by CEOs with more job-hopping experience exhibit higher supplier and customer concentration. Upstream, CEOs devote less attention to alternative supplier search, reflected in fewer tender projects and lower procurement-related recruitment, concentrating purchases among established suppliers. Downstream, CEOs give lower priority to market expansion, reflected in lower advertising expenditure and sales- and marketing-related recruitment, concentrating sales among established customers. CEOs’ R&D experience strengthens the supplier-side association, whereas their production-line experience strengthens the customer-side association. Both associations are stronger in non-state-owned firms and those facing greater performance pressure or higher capital intensity, while board production-line experience weakens the customer-side association. Originality/value This study extends supply chain relationship research beyond transactional and firm-level determinants by highlighting CEO career history as an explanation for firms’ different purchasing and sales patterns across trading partners. We extend the attention-based view by showing how experiences accumulated across organizational boundaries shape managerial attention, adding a historical dimension to managerial priorities. By linking managerial attention to observable supplier search and customer development activities, we clarify how CEO career history translates into supply chain relationship management and how prior functional experience shapes this process.

title: Place Matters: A Dynamic Multilevel Perspective on Stigma Management in French Elderly Care
authors: Claire Le Breton; Frédéric Bally; Albane Grandazzi; Hélène Picard
affiliations: Grenoble Ecole de Management; KEDGE Business School
abstract: Abstract This article interrogates how ‘place’ contributes to managing stigma and its associated multilevel processes. In doing so, it addresses a literature that often treats stigma as a static attribute, overlooking the spatial and material dynamics of managing it. Drawing on a 2.5‐year case study of Help@hom, a French national initiative aimed at restructuring elderly care, we examine how spatial and material arrangements actively shape stigma management processes. We identify three interrelated mechanisms – expanding , enclosing , and fragmenting – through which Help@hom reconfigures the meanings, locations, and materialities of care. Building on these mechanisms, we theorize place as producing, sustaining, and distributing the dynamics of stigma management: place produces stigma management strategies rather than merely providing their setting, sustains stigma by relocating rather than dissolving it, and distributes it across organizational, occupational, and individual levels. Our study demonstrates that place is constitutive of stigma management, shaping how organizations enact and experience multilevel stigma processes, and that spatial and material interventions can produce unexpected cross‐level consequences. In doing so, it advances recent efforts to conceptualize stigma as relational, dynamic, and systemic, and offers a more integrated understanding of how organizations navigate complex stigma management landscapes.

title: May I Have Your Attention, Please? Debating the Ontology of Attention in Organizational Research
authors: Paolo Aversa; Christopher Wickert
affiliations: King's Business School, King's College London; School of Business and Economics Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam
abstract: Abstract Few constructs in management research have proved as generative as organizational attention, and few have been left so largely unexamined at their core. This Point‐Counterpoint debate brings a dormant question into the open: what exactly is attention? The Point argues for an ontological reorientation of the Attention‐Based View from attention quantity to attention quality, reconceptualizing attention as a set of sociomaterial practices of attending that are crescive and differentiated rather than limited and homogeneous. One Counterpoint defends the ontological integrity of attention as scarce, selective, and situated, warning that a crescive ontology dissolves the very constraint from which attention derives its explanatory power. The other Counterpoint charts an expansive third way, tracing the contested assumptions to Herbert Simon's legacy and proposing to broaden the Attention‐Based View towards competition, thicker situations, and possible attentional abundance. In this introduction to the debate, we present the three positions and reflect on what their disagreement teaches us about ontological disputes in management theory more generally. We distil three tests – of phenomena, of explanation, and of genealogy – that scholars can apply when deciding whether a construct's ontology deserves revision, defence, or expansion.

title: From Managerial to Relational Epistemologies: Decolonizing Sustainability Education
authors: Subhabrata Bobby Banerjee
affiliations: Bayes Business School City St George's, University of London London UK
abstract: Abstract In this paper, I critically interrogate the epistemic foundations of sustainability education in business schools in the context of escalating climate crises. I argue that business education is complicit in the production and perpetuation of planetary destruction by privileging market‐based, growth‐driven rationalities while simultaneously co‐opting sustainability discourses to reinforce capitalist accumulation. These dominant managerialist regimes are epistemically resistant to the transformations required for sustainability and climate justice. Drawing on insights from decolonial scholarship and critical pedagogy, I explore the (im)possibilities of epistemic transformations that are needed for a more meaningful engagement with sustainability. I argue that such a transformation requires a shift from managerial to relational epistemologies—ways of knowing that emerge through relationships rather than detached observation of isolated, independent entities. Sustainability, from a relational epistemological perspective, cannot be divorced from social and environmental justice and must also confront power dynamics that drive inequality, neocolonialism and the exploitation of marginalized communities. I propose a radical reimagining of sustainability education—one that historicizes, denaturalizes and problematizes sustainability while prioritizing climate justice, relational ethics and pluriversal futures.

title:
The entrepreneur as ecosystem architect: Economic foundations for strategic entrepreneurship in the age of
                    <scp>AI</scp>
authors: David J. Teece
affiliations: Graduate School University of California, Berkeley Berkeley California USA; Berkeley Research Group Emeryville California USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary This paper develops an alternative foundation for understanding strategic entrepreneurship in the age of artificial intelligence (AI) by joining entrepreneurship research with the profiting from innovation model and the dynamic capabilities framework. It argues that the economic function of the entrepreneur is increasingly that of an ecosystem architect, exercising judgment under uncertainty to orchestrate complementary assets and capabilities across organizational boundaries. AI dramatically lowers the cost of building software thereby lowering product development costs but may raise the barriers to scaling and sustaining competitive advantage. Value capture depends not simply on innovation, but on a compelling value proposition and access to and control over critical complementary assets, architectural control points, and shifting ecosystem bottlenecks. The paper emphasizes that entrepreneurial success requires dynamic capabilities and human judgment to configure and reconfigure ecosystems as technologies and competitive conditions evolve. Managerial Summary AI makes it easier to start a business as it lowers the cost of software development; but building a durable competitive advantage still requires more than a good product or technology. It requires a compelling value proposition to the customer and participation in ecosystems first as tenant and later as anchor. Accordingly, entrepreneurs need to become sophisticated ecosystem players and aspire to be architects, coordinating partners, platforms, data, technology, capital, and other capabilities they may not own. They should identify early which complementary assets are critical to creating and capturing value, understand where control and bottlenecks lie in their ecosystem, and continually reassess these as technology and competition change. AI can help small teams move faster and operate at greater scale, but it does not replace human judgment. Successful entrepreneurs must combine AI with strong ecosystem relationships, domain expertise, governance, and the ability to adapt as their businesses scale.

title: Two margins of allocation and the trend in authorship inequality: Comment on Orhan, van Rossenberg, and Bal (2026)
authors: Christopher I. Rider
affiliations: Ross School of Business, University of Michigan
abstract: Abstract Orhan, van Rossenberg, and Bal (2026; hereafter ORB) report that authorship inequality in management, human resource management, and industrial-organizational psychology journals rose between 1980–1999 and 2000–2019. Their claim that “a small group of researchers has accumulated disproportionate influence over time” carries one intellectual burden, that advantage in obtaining publication opportunities increased; their interpretation of the rise as elite dominance carries a second, that the increase is inequitable. I address the first burden, on which the second depends. Because ORB compute Gini coefficients over researchers with at least one publication, they measure inequality in authorships (i.e., the intensive margin) conditional on publishing (i.e., the extensive margin), and because publication records include neither manuscript submissions nor editorial decisions, such records cannot establish that advantage increased. I demonstrate that inequality across the researchers who compete for publication opportunities rose if and only if that competing pool grew faster than field-specific thresholds of 1.2× to 2.8×, growth that publication records alone cannot substantiate. Meeting the first burden requires journal submission and decision data, which would also show whether authors differ in acceptance rates, in submissions, or in both, and so direct any intervention to its cause.

title: Individual perception of bias in grant peer review strongly associated with openness towards the introduction of lotteries
authors: Christophe Heger
affiliations: Deutsches Zentrum für Hochschul- und Wissenschaftsforschung (DZHW)
abstract: Abstract This study of a representative sample of scientists at German universities and higher educa-tion institutions investigates researchers’ individual perception of bias in grant peer review and their openness towards the potential introduction of grant lotteries, as well as the poten-tial link between the two concepts. Indeed, bias in peer review is often cited in the theoretical debate on grant lotteries. But even though researchers are both very involved in and strongly affected by grant decision-making, there is not enough empirical evidence on their perspec-tive. I find that bias perception is very prevalent, openness is generally rare and researchers who perceive more bias in grant peer review are more open towards grant lotteries in a sub-stantial and statistically significant way.

title: Trended Momentum
authors: Charlie Xiaowu Cai; Peng Li; Kevin Keasey
affiliations: University of Liverpool Management School; University of Bath School of Management; University of Leeds Leeds University Business School
abstract: Abstract Drawing on cognitive psychology and behavioral theories of pattern recognition and heuristic processing, we offer a new perspective on momentum by highlighting how clear price trends shape investor expectations. Trend clarity (TC) materially strengthens momentum returns: the highest trend-clarity quintile earns annualized returns of 12.68%, compared with 6.90% for a conventional momentum strategy. We also show that TC affects momentum trading intensity within Hong and Stein’s (1999) multiperiod return-chasing model. Additional tests indicate that trading on clear trends is a central feature of momentum, distinct from existing explanations and observable across asset classes and global markets.

title: Prospect Theory and Currency Returns: Empirical Evidence
authors: Qi Xu; Roman Kozhan; Mark P. Taylor
affiliations: Zhejiang University: School of Economics and Academy of Financial Research; University of Warwick: Warwick Business School; Washington University in Saint Louis
abstract: Abstract We empirically investigate the role of prospect theory in the foreign exchange market. A currency-level measure of prospect-theory value, constructed from the historical distribution of exchange rate returns, negatively forecasts future currency excess returns. A long–short strategy based on this measure yields approximately 5% per annum. Predictability is stronger when arbitrage is limited. Bank order flow is positively associated with prospect-theory value, with inter-dealer and proprietary trading primarily driving this relation. Funds trade against prospect-theory value, acting as arbitrageurs. Overall, our findings suggest that investors evaluate currencies based on historical return distributions, consistent with prospect theory.

title: The Impact of Mandatory Audit Firm Rotation on Competitive Pricing Strategies for New Audit Engagements: Evidence From the European Union
authors: Ditmir Sufaj; Simon Dekeyser; Marleen Willekens
affiliations: KU Leuven Leuven Belgium
abstract: ABSTRACT Mandatory audit firm rotation was introduced in the European Union (EU), in part, to make the audit market more dynamic by bringing audit engagements to market more frequently. However, it creates a countervailing economic force: By limiting the duration of auditor–client relationships, mandatory rotation shortens the period over which auditors can recoup first‐year fee discounts through fees earned in subsequent years. Consistent with this argument, we find that first‐year fee discounts decline substantially after mandatory firm rotation took effect in the EU, particularly in countries with stricter limits on auditor tenure. Thus, greater opportunities to compete for new engagements do not necessarily translate into greater first‐year fee discounts. Our findings highlight that regulators should consider not only how frequently audit engagements are brought to market but also how limits on auditor tenure shape the pricing incentives associated with competing for new clients.

title: The Limit of Nature: Thucydides and the Politics of Theory
authors: MARK D. FISHER
affiliations: Georgetown University
abstract: This article reconsiders Thucydides’s role as a foundational theorist of human nature. Contrary to conventional readings, I argue that Thucydides approaches “nature” ( physis ) less as a universal principle of behavior than as a site of political and theoretical investigation. By distinguishing his authorial voice from those of his speakers, I demonstrate that his analysis consistently approaches human nature as a limit concept—a baseline and boundary of human capacity that emerges in moments of existential precarity—while introducing a more nuanced set of terms to describe the habitual behaviors of political groups. By nevertheless foregrounding the more robust and determinative concept of nature in moments of contentious deliberation, Thucydides encourages reflection on the political dynamics that generate essentialist theories in public discourse. His account thus serves as a helpful point of reference for thinking about how competitive, polarizing speech affects the substantive categories of political debate and analysis, and through them political action.

title: How Sociotropic Aesthetic Judgments Drive Opposition to Dense Housing Development
authors: DAVID E. BROOCKMAN; CHRISTOPHER S. ELMENDORF; JOSHUA L. KALLA
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley; University of California, Davis; Yale University
abstract: Voter opposition to dense housing development contributes to America’s housing shortage. Prevailing explanations emphasize homeowner self-interest and “NIMBYism.” We develop a theory of how sociotropic aesthetic judgments shape housing policy preferences and demonstrate its unique implications with a series of descriptive studies and experiments. First, people who choose to live in dense neighborhoods have an aesthetic taste for density, leading homeowners in already-dense areas to be more supportive of dense development both in their neighborhoods and elsewhere. Second, voters are more supportive of dense development when it is proposed in already-dense neighborhoods where it “fits”—even voters who live in those same dense neighborhoods. Finally, genuine aesthetic distaste for tall buildings is widespread and causally affects support for development. Our findings offer a new lens for understanding housing policy preferences and suggest novel solutions for addressing America’s housing shortage.
